name: Tria Beauty hair removal laser

lead: The Tria is a consumer diode laser for hair removal at home, used for longer-lasting hair reduction than shaving provides. According to Wikipedia, it is one of two diode devices the US FDA had cleared for over-the-counter sale as of 2025, and the clearance covers hair reduction.

Laser energy is absorbed by melanin in the hair and heats the follicle, damaging it while sparing most surrounding skin (selective photothermolysis). Clinic laser hair removal is described as producing long-term reduction rather than total removal, usually needing several sessions.

paras: Users treat shaved skin in sessions repeated over weeks to months, then maintain as needed. Dark, coarse hair on lighter skin responds best.
Common effects are redness, itching and swelling lasting a few days; burns, pigment changes and eye injury are possible. Light, grey, red and fine hair respond poorly.

angle.text: Users buy the Tria as an at-home diode laser for longer-lasting hair reduction than shaving. Laser energy is absorbed by hair pigment and damages the follicles over repeated sessions. It is one of two over-the-counter diode lasers the FDA had cleared as of 2025, for hair reduction.

lead: The Tria is a hand-held diode laser for hair removal at home. People use it on the legs, underarms, bikini line, face and body to reduce hair growth and get smoother skin without repeated salon visits, waxing or daily shaving. It was developed by SpectraGenics, later renamed TRIA Beauty, and first cleared by the FDA for over-the-counter use in February 2008; a second clearance in January 2010 added permanent hair reduction labeling.[1][2]

Professional laser hair removal works by selective photothermolysis: light absorbed by melanin heats the follicle while sparing most surrounding skin.[3] FDA clearance for "permanent hair reduction" refers to a long-term decrease in regrowth, not total removal.[3] Dark, coarse hair on light skin responds best, and most people need at least eight treatments.[3] Wikipedia states that as of 2025 two diode devices, the Epilaser and the TRIA, were cleared for over-the-counter sale.[3]
infobox: Dark, coarse hair on light skin[3]

paras: The second-generation 2009 model used an AlGaAs diode array at 810 nm, about 40 W, with five output levels from 6 to 22 J/cm2, a 10 mm spot, a weight of about 1.36 lb and Class I classification.[4] The manufacturer says its current 4X model only fires after a skin-tone safety check and is cleared for adults aged 18 and over.[5]

SpectraGenics announced FDA over-the-counter clearance for its hand-held diode laser in February 2008 and relaunched the product in February 2009 as TRIA, billed as the first FDA-cleared at-home laser sold to consumers.[2][4] A late-2009 second generation added power settings and cut the price 40% from the original $595 in the company's account.[1] The company called a January 2010 clearance for permanent hair reduction labeling the first for an at-home device.[1][2]

Trade press noted that Palomar Medical Technologies had received FDA approval for an at-home system developed with Procter & Gamble in late 2006 that was never commercialised, and Palomar sued TRIA in June 2009 alleging patent infringement.[4]

The 2009 suggested schedule was one treatment every other week for three months, then monthly for three to five months.[4] A Beautylish adviser who used the 4X on the upper lip and underarms for several months described minimal pain, sessions of 15 to 45 minutes depending on the area, a rise to energy level 3 or 4, and a "very slight difference" so far; she advised shaving first and keeping skin clean and lotion-free, and said it works best on light brown to black hair.[6]

Common short-lived effects of laser hair removal include redness, swelling and itching; more serious ones include acne flare-ups, skin discoloration, burns, infection and scabbing.[3] The manufacturer states the laser targets melanin and is therefore not suitable or effective for everyone, notably limited by hair colour.[5]

No studies found. The company's 2010 announcement describes the device as "clinically proven" but cites only a Dermatology Times survey of dermatologists in its release.[1] For laser hair removal as a category, a randomized trial reported 69.2% hair reduction with a diode laser versus 52.7% with intense pulsed light at 12 months.[3]

timeline.event: The FDA approves laser hair removal for "permanent hair reduction" in professional devices.[3]
SpectraGenics announces first FDA OTC clearance for its at-home diode laser.[2]
Relaunched as TRIA; second generation launches later in the year at a lower price; Palomar files patent suit.[4]
Additional FDA clearance for permanent hair reduction labeling.[1]
Wikipedia lists TRIA and Epilaser as the two FDA-cleared OTC diode devices.[3]
